draft.title: Sound devices
card: Alliteration
repeats the first consonant sound in nearby words. In "the wind whipped wildly", the w sound repeats.
Assonance
repeats a vowel sound in nearby words, even if the spelling differs. In "the moan of the slow, cold road", the long o sound repeats.
Onomatopoeia
uses a word that imitates the sound it names, such as crash, hiss or thud.
Effect
Sound changes pace and mood. Sharp sounds like t and k can make a line quick and tense. Long, soft sounds can slow a line and make it calm or sad.
draft.remember: Sound devices shape how fast a line moves and what mood it carries.

opts: The tired kite drifted high in the night
The wet wind wandered through the woods
The kettle hissed and the pipes clanged
Rain fell on the roof of the old shed
a.why: The long i sound repeats in tired, kite, high and night, and that is assonance. The second option repeats the w consonant at the start of words, which is alliteration. The third uses imitating words, which is onomatopoeia.
a.clue: Listen for a repeated vowel sound, not a first letter.

b.q: A writer describes a calm evening: "The soft, slow waves sighed and slid over the sand." What is the main effect of the repeated s sound?
opts: It slows the line and creates a gentle, peaceful mood
It speeds the line up and creates a tense, urgent mood
It imitates the sound of a loud crash on the shore
It repeats a vowel sound to create a sense of anger
b.why: The repeated soft s sound is alliteration. It makes the line flow slowly and gently, which suits a calm evening. The tense option is tempting because repeated sounds can speed a line up, but sharp sounds do that, not soft ones.
b.clue: Think about whether the s sound is sharp or soft.

a.best: The tired kite drifted high in the night

b.best: It slows the line and creates a gentle, peaceful mood

problems.detail: The distractor 'Rain fell on the roof of the old shed' repeats a short e sound in 'fell' and 'shed', so a student could argue it shows weak assonance. The why (a) does not explain why this option is wrong. Consider a distractor with no repeated vowel sound.
The stem tells students the scene is 'a calm evening', which points straight to the 'gentle, peaceful' option. The question tests matching words more than the effect of the sound.

Effect
Sound changes pace and mood, not just how a line sounds. Sharp sounds like t and k can make a line quick and tense. Soft sounds like s and l, and long vowels, can slow a line and make it calm or sad.
proposal.remember: Sound devices shape how fast a line moves and what mood it carries.

opts: The tired kite drifted high in the night
The wet wind wandered through the woods
The kettle hissed and the pipes clanged
Her cousin found a map in the drawer
a.why: The long i sound repeats in tired, kite, high and night, and that is assonance. The second option repeats the w consonant at the start of words, which is alliteration, and the third uses imitating words, which is onomatopoeia. The last line has no repeated vowel or first consonant sound at all.
a.clue: Listen for a repeated vowel sound, not a first letter.

b.q: A writer describes the sea: "The waves slid across the sand and settled." What is the main effect of the repeated s sound?
opts: It slows the line and gives it a soft, calm mood
It speeds the line up and makes the mood tense
It imitates the sound of waves crashing on rocks
It only makes the line sound pleasant to read
b.why: The repeated s is a soft sound that draws the line out, so it slows the pace and calms the mood. The tense option is tempting because repeated sounds can speed a line up, but sharp sounds like t and k do that, not soft ones. Saying it only sounds pleasant misses that sound changes pace and mood.
b.clue: Is the s sound sharp or soft?
